overview.title: What is ansible-core?
overview.introduction: ansible-core is the minimal automation engine at the center of Ansible automation. Developers and automation content authors use it to build, test, troubleshoot, and validate inventories, playbooks, roles, plugins, and collections before moving approved content into an operational workflow.

items.title: Built-in command-line tools
items.detail: The package installs commands for running playbooks, inspecting inventory and configuration, reading documentation, installing collections, encrypting sensitive data, and testing automation content. These include ansible, ansible-playbook, ansible-inventory, ansible-config, ansible-doc, ansible-galaxy, ansible-vault, and ansible-test.

items.title: Automation language
items.detail: ansible-core processes playbooks written in YAML. Playbooks can contain tasks, handlers, variables, conditions, loops, imports, and includes.

items.title: Execution runtime
items.detail: It reads inventory, connects to managed nodes, loads the required plugins, and runs modules. The same engine can be invoked from a developer's terminal or through a controller.

items.title: Built-in content
items.detail: It includes the modules and plugins in the ansible.builtin namespace. This content ships with ansible-core and does not require a separate collection installation.

items.title: Additional collections
items.detail: Install collections separately when your automation needs modules, plugins, roles, or other content that is not included in ansible.builtin.

overview.note: In the following demonstrations, you will install, inspect, and validate a local ansible-core runtime. Teams that need shared credentials, controlled access, approvals, scheduling, and audit history should run approved production jobs through a controller or orchestration platform. The platform manages the workflow; an Ansible runtime executes the automation.

orchestrationOptions.title: Common platforms for shared Ansible operations
orchestrationOptions.introduction: These platforms provide a shared interface for running automation, controlling access, and reviewing job results. Their scope, Ansible integration, and support models differ.

items.title: Automation Controller
items.detail: The Red Hat-supported enterprise controller included with Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform. It provides centralized credentials, access controls, job templates, workflows, schedules, APIs, job history, and auditing.

items.title: AWX
items.detail: The upstream community project from which Automation Controller is developed. It provides a web interface, REST API, and task engine for Ansible. AWX is self-supported, so review its release, deployment, and upgrade model before using it in production.

items.title: Semaphore UI
items.detail: A self-hosted web interface and API for running Ansible and other automation tools. It provides projects, repositories, inventories, protected credentials, task templates, schedules, logs, and role-based access. Community and commercial editions are available.

items.title: Rundeck
items.detail: A runbook automation platform that can include Ansible in larger operational workflows. Its Ansible integration can import inventory and run modules or playbooks. Rundeck manages the workflow while Ansible performs the Ansible-specific execution.

orchestrationOptions.note: Check how each platform handles execution isolation, secrets, permissions, approvals, audit records, availability, scaling, upgrades, integrations, and support. Links to dedicated HODs can be added as those demonstrations are published.

relatedTools.title: ansible-dev-tools
relatedTools.detail: ansible-dev-tools is a curated toolkit installed separately from ansible-core for developing, linting, testing, building, signing, and running Ansible content. HOD 002 introduces the included tools, including ansible-navigator, and compares the upstream Python distribution with the Red Hat delivery path.

prerequisites.label: System
prerequisites.detail: A current RHEL 9 physical or virtual machine.

prerequisites.label: Access
prerequisites.detail: A user that can run administrative commands with sudo.

prerequisites.label: Connectivity
prerequisites.detail: Outbound access to Red Hat registration and content services for every demo, plus PyPI for the upstream pip and pipx workflows. Configure any required proxy and trusted certificate chain before starting.

prerequisites.label: Starting state
prerequisites.detail: Begin each demonstration from a separate, fully updated RHEL 9 system where ansible-core is not already installed. Do not run the three workflows sequentially on the same unchanged VM.

prerequisiteCallouts.title: Don’t have a Red Hat subscription?
paragraphs: You can join the Red Hat Developer program at no cost. Eligible members can activate the self-supported Red Hat Developer Subscription for Individuals, which provides access to RHEL and repositories such as BaseOS and AppStream. You do not need an Ansible Automation Platform subscription to complete this lab. Repository access does not create a Red Hat support entitlement for automation you create with ansible-core.

prerequisiteCallouts.title: Why do the upstream demonstrations register RHEL?
paragraphs: Demo 02 and Demo 03 register RHEL only to obtain Python 3.12 and its pip package from supported RHEL repositories. The ansible-core package is downloaded separately from PyPI.

A Red Hat subscription is therefore required for the demonstrated RHEL package source, not for access to upstream ansible-core itself. On another Linux distribution, use that distribution’s supported method to install a compatible Python runtime.

prerequisiteDetails.title: Enterprise environment considerations
prerequisiteDetails.introduction: Open this guidance when the demonstration is being adapted for organization-managed, restricted, or disconnected systems.

items.title: Registering systems in a managed environment
paragraphs: The demonstrations use an interactive Red Hat account login because each learner is registering one disposable system. For repeatable provisioning at organizational scale, Red Hat also supports registering RHEL with an activation key and organization ID. Treat activation keys as protected provisioning credentials: do not place them in source control, reusable machine images, terminal recordings, or unprotected scripts.

The rhc workflow can connect a system to Subscription Management, Red Hat Lightspeed inventory, and remote host configuration. Before registering an organizational system, confirm which services are permitted and whether its inventory data, system-purpose settings, and remote-management capabilities meet your security, privacy, and operations policies.

items.title: Using controlled or disconnected content sources
paragraphs: The recorded workflows use direct HTTPS connections to Red Hat services and, for the upstream installations, PyPI. Treat them as connected reference workflows. In a restricted or disconnected environment, use the sources approved by your organization, such as Satellite-managed RHEL content, a controlled Python package index, and an approved Galaxy or Automation Hub server.

The installation ownership and compatibility decisions remain the same, but repository registration, proxy, certificate, package-index, and collection-source configuration will differ. Validate the mirrored artifacts and dependencies before promoting them between development, test, and production environments.

items.title: Retiring the lab system
paragraphs: Removing ansible-core and running rhc disconnect are local cleanup actions, not a complete organizational asset-retirement process. For a managed or disposable system, also follow your organization’s process for reviewing and removing retired host records from the applicable inventory, subscription-management, security, and configuration-management services.

supportGuidance.title: Get help from the right owner
supportGuidance.introduction: Route a problem according to the component that owns it. Before opening a case or issue, reproduce the failure, remove credentials and private infrastructure details from the output, and collect the package, runtime, configuration, and content evidence that identifies the failing layer.

routes.title: RHEL registration, repositories, or RPM
routes.detail: Start with Red Hat documentation and your organization’s RHEL support path. Open a Red Hat case only when the system has the applicable entitlement and the issue falls within the documented support scope.

routes.title: Upstream ansible-core or PyPI package
routes.detail: Use your organization’s Python or open-source support process first. For a reproducible upstream defect, review the Ansible project’s issue guidance and search existing issues before filing a new report.

routes.title: Collection, module, or plugin
routes.detail: Use the FQCN and collection version to identify the content owner. Check that collection’s documentation, support statement, changelog, and issue tracker rather than assuming every content failure belongs to ansible-core.

routes.title: Local environment or approved package source
routes.detail: Contact the team that owns the control node, Python runtime, proxy, certificates, controlled package index, or mirrored repositories. Provide the selected installation path and the evidence below so ownership can be established quickly.

diagnostics.title: Collect evidence before requesting help
diagnostics.introduction: Run the commands that apply to your installation path. Review and redact the output before sharing it; do not include passwords, activation keys, account identifiers, tokens, or private infrastructure details.

comparisons.title: RHEL-provided ansible-core compatibility
comparisons.introduction: RHEL packages ansible-core with a control-node Python runtime selected for each RHEL major release. Managed-host requirements depend on the operating system, connection method, module, and collection. The table covers the ansible-core technical runtime baseline for Linux, Unix, and Windows hosts; it is not a complete Red Hat support matrix for every managed platform, collection, or automation use case. Individual collections and modules can set narrower requirements. It lists feature streams rather than exact RPM builds, so the installed 2.14.z or 2.16.z version can change through updates. Red Hat maintains these RPMs under the RHEL lifecycle, independently of the upstream lifecycle.

notes.title: Linux and Unix hosts
notes.detail: Ansible is not installed on the managed host. Most modules need one supported Python interpreter from the range or alternatives listed below; the host does not need every Python version shown. It also needs an account that Ansible can reach over SSH. When a task must run as root, that account needs permission to use sudo or another configured become method. The ansible.builtin.raw module can help bootstrap a host that does not yet have Python.

notes.title: Windows hosts
notes.detail: Windows modules run through Windows PowerShell rather than Python. The host also needs a supported Windows release and a configured connection. The versioned ansible-core guidance shown here uses WinRM; individual modules can require a newer Windows, PowerShell, or .NET Framework version.

notes.title: Network devices and appliances
notes.detail: Network modules commonly use collection-specific connection plugins and do not require Python on the managed device. Check the collection, module, connection-plugin, operating-system, and device-vendor documentation for additional transport, library, firmware, or platform requirements.

comparisons.title: Choose your ansible-core installation path
comparisons.introduction: Make this choice in three stages. First identify the collections, platforms, and controller-side dependencies required by your automation. Next decide who will provide, maintain, and support a compatible ansible-core: Red Hat through a RHEL RPM or the upstream Ansible project through PyPI. If you choose the upstream distribution, then select the environment model that fits the way the control node will be used.

notes.title: Start with the automation requirements
notes.detail: List the collections and platforms the control node must support before selecting ansible-core. Find their requirements in the collection documentation and release notes. A collection’s meta/runtime.yml file can declare its compatible ansible-core range through requires_ansible; other Python, system, and platform requirements are collection-specific. The newest ansible-core release is not automatically compatible with every collection or existing automation project.

reference.label: Read about the requires_ansible collection constraint

notes.title: What stays the same
notes.detail: Both distributions provide the ansible-core command-line tools, automation language, execution runtime, and embedded ansible.builtin collection. Other collections are installed and maintained separately.

notes.title: Package access and product support are different
notes.detail: A RHEL subscription provides access to the AppStream RPM. It does not automatically create support coverage for every playbook, module, collection, or automation use case. Check the documented Red Hat support scope before making a production decision.

reference.label: Read Red Hat's ansible-core support scope

comparisons.summaryLabel: Decision 2: Compare distribution and support models

values: Red Hat builds and signs the RPM. DNF installs it from RHEL AppStream and owns its files, dependencies, signatures, updates, errata, and removal.
The upstream Ansible project publishes the Python distribution on PyPI. Install it with pip in a virtual environment or use pipx to create a dedicated application environment.
DNF selects the RHEL filesystem locations and platform Python dependencies. The commands are normally available system-wide and remain under RPM control.

You select a supported Python interpreter and own the installation environment, dependencies, upgrades, and removal. Keep PyPI packages out of RHEL's platform Python and separate from any RPM-managed ansible-core installation.

The enabled RHEL Application Stream determines the feature line. RHEL 9 provides the ansible-core 2.14 Full Life Application Stream, and Red Hat can update the RPM while retaining that feature baseline.

Upstream normally publishes a new X.Y feature release about every six months and X.Y.Z patch releases about every four weeks. New features and support for newer Python versions become available here first.
Maintenance follows the RHEL and AppStream lifecycle. Red Hat can backport fixes without changing the upstream feature version, so use Red Hat advisories and security data when assessing the package.

The upstream project maintains three X.Y releases at graduated levels. The newest receives general bug and security fixes, the next receives critical and security fixes, and the oldest receives security fixes. Unmaintained releases generally receive no further fixes.
Use the Python dependencies selected by DNF. Do not apply the upstream PyPI control-node matrix to this installation.

Choose a maintained ansible-core release that supports the Python interpreter in the environment. Test playbooks before changing X.Y releases because complete compatibility between feature releases is not guaranteed.

Red Hat supports the RPM for its documented scope, including playbooks, roles, and modules included with or generated by specified Red Hat products. Broader support for the Ansible platform and core-maintained modules requires the applicable Ansible Automation Platform entitlement.

Maintained releases receive updates, documentation, issue tracking, and community collaboration from the upstream project. Installing ansible-core from PyPI does not create a Red Hat product-support entitlement.

reference.label: Read Red Hat's ansible-core support scope

decisionGuide.label: Decision 3
decisionGuide.title: Choose the environment model
decisionGuide.introduction: After choosing the distribution, match its environment model to the way the control node will be maintained. The upstream distribution has two useful isolation patterns; they solve different operational problems.

options.title: RHEL AppStream RPM
options.label: Operating-system managed
options.detail: DNF manages the system-wide command, RHEL-integrated Python dependencies, signed updates, and removal. No environment activation is required.
options.bestFor: RHEL-integrated use where DNF ownership and the documented Red Hat support scope are the priorities.

options.title: pip with a virtual environment
options.label: Project managed
options.detail: You choose the Python interpreter and manage ansible-core with related controller-side Python libraries in a project-owned environment. Activate that environment before using its commands.
options.bestFor: Project development, testing, or CI where the interpreter and Python dependencies must be controlled and reproduced together.

options.title: pipx
options.label: User managed
options.detail: pipx creates a dedicated application environment and exposes the Ansible commands on the user's PATH, so manual activation is normally unnecessary.
options.bestFor: An individual's command-line environment where convenient isolation and direct command access are the priorities.
options.note: pipx isolates ansible-core and its Python dependencies, not the complete Ansible runtime. Configuration, inventory, playbooks, roles, and collections can remain outside the pipx environment. Add controller-side Python libraries with pipx inject or pipx runpip; manage required operating-system libraries separately.

path.condition: Want RHEL and DNF to own the installation?
Need project-specific Python dependencies, activation, or CI reproducibility?
path.result: Choose pip with a virtual environment.

items.title: Content compatibility
items.detail: Confirm that the collections required by the automation support the selected ansible-core version.

items.title: Runtime compatibility
items.detail: Confirm that the selected ansible-core and control-node Python versions are compatible.

items.title: Installation ownership
items.detail: Know whether DNF, a project virtual environment, or pipx owns and updates the installation.

items.title: Source and maintenance
items.detail: Know where the packages come from and how the selected installation will receive updates.

items.title: Keep one package owner
items.detail: Allow DNF, a project virtual environment, or pipx to own a particular ansible-core installation. Do not let multiple package managers modify the same runtime.

items.title: Protect RHEL’s platform Python
items.detail: Do not install ansible-core or additional PyPI packages into the Python environment used by the operating system.

items.title: Do not overwrite the RPM
items.detail: Use a separate virtual environment or pipx when installing upstream ansible-core on a system that also contains the RHEL RPM.

items.title: Check command precedence
items.detail: If more than one installation exists, use type -a ansible, command -v ansible, and ansible --version to confirm which executable and Python runtime are active.

items.title: Understand the pipx boundary
items.detail: pipx isolates ansible-core and its Python dependencies. It does not automatically isolate Ansible configuration, inventory, playbooks, collections, credentials, or operating-system libraries.

items.title: Use independent environments for comparison
items.detail: Perform the three demonstrations on separate clean systems or restored snapshots. They are alternative installation paths, not three installations that should normally be combined on one control node.

followups.title: What does the localhost test validate?
paragraphs: The final ansible.builtin.ping command uses a local connection. It confirms that the selected Ansible executable starts, loads the module, and can execute it with the specified local Python interpreter.

This test does not validate connectivity to a managed host, inventory design, SSH, WinRM, network-device access, credentials, privilege escalation, DNS, firewall rules, or the runtime requirements of additional collections. Those checks belong to a managed-host demonstration.

comparisons.takeaway: These installation methods create a local control-node runtime. They do not provide an immutable team runtime, centralized credentials, role-based access, scheduling, or audit history. Use an execution environment and an appropriate controller or orchestration platform when those production requirements apply.

comparisons.title: Plan the operational lifecycle
comparisons.introduction: An installation method also establishes an ownership and change model. Decide who monitors updates, records the approved baseline, tests feature-line changes, performs recovery, and removes retired installations before the control node becomes shared or long-lived.

notes.title: Treat maintenance updates and feature-line changes differently
notes.detail: A maintenance update stays within an ansible-core X.Y line. Moving to another feature line can change controller and managed-host Python requirements, remove deprecated behavior, and require content changes. Review the matching porting guide and test inventories, playbooks, roles, plugins, collections, and representative managed hosts before switching.

notes.title: ansible-core and collections have separate lifecycles
notes.detail: Updating ansible-core does not automatically update collections installed with ansible-galaxy. Record and test collection versions separately, together with any Python or operating-system libraries they require. A requirements file can describe collection versions, but it does not replace the Python dependency record for the selected runtime.

pipx stores metadata used by reinstall operations, but that metadata is not a complete runtime snapshot. Reliable recovery requires the previously recorded package specification, interpreter, injected dependencies, collections, and external configuration.

comparisons.title: Pin versions for a repeatable environment
comparisons.introduction: A version choice becomes an operational baseline only after it is recorded at the right level. Pin what has been tested, keep the source of each component visible, and change the baseline deliberately rather than allowing a fresh installation to resolve a different set of packages.

notes.title: A feature-line constraint is not an exact pin
notes.detail: The expression ansible-core==2.21.* allows any published maintenance release in the 2.21 feature line. It is useful while learning or selecting the newest compatible maintenance build, but separate installations performed at different times can resolve different versions. Use an exact value such as ansible-core==2.21.4 after that release has passed your tests.

notes.title: Requirements and constraints do different jobs
notes.detail: A requirements file tells pip what to install. A constraints file limits versions selected for packages required by that installation, but naming a package in a constraints file does not install it. Keep the direct installation requirement visible and use constraints when several environments must obey the same version limits.

notes.title: Pinning ansible-core alone does not pin the runtime
notes.detail: A repeatable baseline also records the control-node Python, transitive Python packages, collections, controller-side libraries, and relevant operating-system dependencies. Inventory, configuration, credentials, and managed-host requirements are operational inputs rather than Python packages and must be governed separately.

notes.title: Use approved artifact sources
notes.detail: Direct access to the Red Hat CDN, PyPI, and Ansible Galaxy is suitable for many individual learning environments. An organization may instead require approved RPM repositories, a controlled Python package index, approved collection sources, trusted certificate authorities, artifact scanning, and promotion between development, test, and production repositories. Record both the package version and its approved source. A version pin controls which release is selected; it does not establish that the downloaded artifact came from a trusted or organization-approved repository.

Put exact package versions in a reviewed requirements file. A tested environment can be captured with python -m pip freeze --all. When stronger artifact verification is needed, use fully pinned requirements with hashes and require those hashes during installation.

A freeze file records the packages resolved in one environment; it does not guarantee that the same wheels or system libraries exist on another operating system or architecture. Rebuild and test the environment on every supported platform.

Install ansible-core and injected Python libraries with exact package specifications. pipx pin ansible-core prevents pipx upgrade and reinstall operations from changing the current environment until it is unpinned. Use pipx list --include-injected to review the application and its additions.

pipx pin holds the existing application environment; it is not a portable lock for collections, configuration, inventory, credentials, or operating-system libraries. Keep those records beside the automation project or build definition.

Declare required collections in requirements.yml and use an exact version such as ==1.2.3 for an accepted baseline. Store the file with the automation content and install it with ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml.

Updating ansible-core does not update collections installed with ansible-galaxy. A collection requirement also does not capture every controller-side Python or operating-system dependency required by its plugins.
